claims.text: Low-temperature annealing of the as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy relieves internal stress.
Low-temperature annealing homogenizes the distribution of magnetic exchange interactions in the FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy.
Stress relief and homogenization of exchange interactions broaden the magnetostructural transition.
Low-temperature annealing reduces hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The initial material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy produced by rapid deposition.
The as-deposited material has a single-phase, ordered hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited material exhibits a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition with pronounced hysteresis.
Annealing modestly below the transformation onset can reduce local compositional and structural inhomogeneities without significant grain growth.
Annealing at approximately 10–20% below the critical transformation temperature for several hours can preserve the hexagonal phase while avoiding disruptive phase changes.
Internal stress and microstructural inhomogeneities control the distribution of magnetic exchange energies.
Heat treatment can reduce the distribution of exchange energies and make a high-entropy alloy more magnetically homogeneous.
Reducing internal strain and exchange-interaction heterogeneity smooths the energetic landscape encountered during low-field cooling.
The annealed alloy will exhibit a more gradual magnetocaloric response over a broader temperature range.
Annealing will decrease the sharp peak in magnetic entropy change.
Annealing will reduce magnetic or thermal hysteresis relative to the as-deposited state.
The as-deposited baseline has limited heat-exchange rates because of its low surface-to-volume ratio.
The annealing response may depend on alloy composition.
Annealing at excessive temperature or duration may cause grain growth or phase decomposition and alter the magnetocaloric response.
Reducing hysteresis may trade off against peak entropy change or refrigerant capacity.
